signals.title: RL infrastructure at Microsoft AI | Microsoft AI
signals.excerpt:
Long, stable, and numerically accurate Reinforcement Learning (RL) is an essential piece of Microsoft AI’s (MAI) path to Humanist Superintelligence. We aim to climb capabilities from the base model through RL itself, which means runs of many thousands of training steps spanning weeks to months on thousands of GPUs, rather than a short RL phase at the end of post-training. Over runs that long, small numerical mismatches and system inefficiencies compound, so we built Rocket, MAI’s in-house RL framework, to enable us to post-train models at increasing scale. We recently shared an update on our new three-trillion-parameter base model, MAI Base 2, in Frontier Pre-training at Microsoft AI. MAI Base 2 is now being post-trained with Rocket, climbing from the base model through RL without distillation from third-party models. This work is separate from the MAI Code 2 models.

...

The MAI Thinking 1 technical report introduced Rocket as the RL framework which post-trained our previous pre-trained model, MAI Base 1, into the reasoning model MAI Thinking 1. Since then, we have improved Rocket to operate at the larger scale demanded by MAI Base 2. RL infrastructure needs to address many challenges at increasing scale:

1. Staleness. Agentic rollouts can take hours while the learner keeps updating the policy. Because GRPO scores each rollout against the others for the same problem, a single slow or failed rollout holds back its entire group, so training drifts further off-policy.
2. Numerical consistency. Fitting a larger model and longer contexts into the sampler requires lower-precision storage, and differences in precision, kernels, and parallelism between the sampler and learner can slow learning and destabilize training.
3. Fault tolerance and elasticity. Runs that span thousands of GPUs for weeks or months will encounter hardware failures, while the best runtime configuration and data mixture change. Restarting the whole job for every failure or reconfiguration wastes GPU time, so the system must recover and reconfigure components while the run continues.

...

Rocket is built for the more demanding case of climbing from base capabilities through RL itself, without a distilled head start. Being able to reach the frontier without depending on other labs’ models is central to MAI’s self-sufficiency. The infrastructure challenges above become the main design constraints rather than edge cases in this regime.

...

We built Rocket to

...

MAI develops and operates three tightly connected systems necessary for RL: the learner and training framework, Rocket, and an inference engine built on an MAI-maintained fork of SGLang. Owning all three allows us to co-design the interfaces between them rather than optimize each component in isolation.

This does not mean building every layer from scratch. Rocket leverages Kubernetes or Slurm to allocate nodes to a job, and Rocket’s components run on Ray as actors. We adopted SGLang as our inference foundation and have substantially adapted it to MAI’s models and long-running agentic RL workloads. Owning these integrations carries a maintenance cost, but lets us evolve the complete RL loop rather than optimize its components in isolation. A future blog post will detail the ways that we adapted SGLang to fit our workloads.

signals.title: Google & MongoDB launch AI agent integration
signals.excerpt:
# Google & MongoDB launch AI agent integration 

 Mon, 23rd Nov 2026 (Yesterday) 

 DAVID SHILOVSKY Interviews Editor 

Google and MongoDB have introduced a MongoDB integration for Google's Agent Development Kit, adding session storage, memory and retrieval features for AI agents.

The software connects MongoDB with Google's open-source ADK framework, which is used to build, debug and deploy AI agents. It is designed to let developers store agent sessions and longer-term memory in MongoDB, while using MongoDB Search to retrieve operational data.

Google's ADK is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin. The new integration centres on ADK 2.0, which Google describes as the orchestration layer for multi-agent systems, with MongoDB providing storage for sessions and memory.

According to the companies, the aim is to give developers a single data layer for application data, agent state and retrieval tasks. This is intended to reduce the need for separate databases or synchronisation pipelines when moving an AI agent from prototype to production.

Session storage

A key part of the release is the MongoDbSessionService class, which stores sessions, events, and application, user and session state in MongoDB. It includes optimistic concurrency control to help applications manage concurrent updates safely, along with configurable collections to fit existing data architectures.

The integration also includes a MongoDbMemoryService class for agents that need memory beyond a single session. It ingests session events into MongoDB collections and retrieves relevant memories through keyword matching.

MongoDB says memory ingestion is idempotent, helping to avoid duplication if an application adds the same session more than once. Developers can use the service to add a session to memory and search stored memory for relevant information tied to a user or application.

Search tools

The release also adds MongoDbToolset support for AI agents that need access to product catalogues, documents or other operational records already stored in MongoDB. This lets agents call search tools within ADK while the application retains control of the database connection, configuration and index settings.

According to the companies, the search component supports semantic and hybrid retrieval. In practice, this means developers can build agents for tasks such as product discovery, knowledge assistance, support workflows and specialised copilots using the same database layer.

Support covers MongoDB Atlas as well as self-managed MongoDB 8.0 and newer deployments for vector and hybrid search. Developers can connect through a connection string or use an existing PyMongo client, and can configure index names, embedding fields, result limits and candidate counts through MongoDbToolSettings.

Production focus

The integration reflects a broader shift in the AI software market as companies try to move agents from demonstrations into operational systems that can preserve user context across multiple interactions. In that environment, session persistence and memory have become central design questions alongside model choice.

Google says ADK supplies the framework and tool interface, while the MongoDB integration provides the persistence layer beneath it. The setup is intended to support agents that maintain conversation history independently of a single machine and carry a user's history across sessions.

The underlying ADK platform integrates with Gemini models, including Gemini 4 Argon for multi-step reasoning and Gemini 3.8 Flash for lower-latency execution. The companies say ADK 2.0 also provides standardised tool-calling interfaces, native telemetry and access controls.

The software can be installed through the Python package manager using the google-adk[mongodb] package, adding MongoDB support directly into ADK development environments.

The integration supports MongoDB Atlas and self-managed MongoDB 8.0+ deployments for vector and hybrid search.

signals.title: Inkling 2 Mini Turns Repeated Computation Into a Local-Model Design Choice · Hugging Face Blog
signals.excerpt:
Inkling 2 Mini contains 24 physical decoder layers. The middle 12 are revisited three times, producing 48 logical layer visits: six initial layers, three passes through the 12-layer core, and six final layers. The repeated passes share weights, with learned messages carrying information between passes. Each visit routes a token to eight experts selected from 128.

This structure separates weight capacity from compute depth. Reusing weights can reduce how many distinct layer parameters must be stored, but every repeated visit still performs work. It also needs runtime state, including attention caches.

...

Alongside the fixed three-pass model, the release includes a research checkpoint that can run the looped core one, two, or three times. Fewer passes are intended to make inference faster, with a possible reduction in output quality. The release authors say they have not evaluated that variant deeply, so it should be treated as an experimental control rather than a guaranteed performance dial.

...

## Local deployment still requires a memory budget

Support spans Transformers, llama.cpp-based tooling, MLX, and SGLang. The release provides four-bit and eight-bit GGUF variants for local runtimes, while MLX can use the original mixed-precision checkpoint. SGLang targets datacenter serving and can optionally use a DSpark draft model for speculative decoding. These options broaden access, but they are not interchangeable representations with identical behavior.

Before downloading weights, estimate four separate budgets:

1. Weight memory: quantization can reduce it, but runtime overhead and model metadata still count.
2. Context memory: a supported maximum is not the same as a practical operating length. Cache use grows with the active sequence and concurrency.
3. Compute time: 48 logical visits remain 48 visits even when some weights are shared.
4. Auxiliary memory: image processing, draft models, server buffers, and concurrent requests add to the total.

signals.title: Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments | Scale Labs
signals.excerpt:
10/5/2026

# Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments

By Edgar Arakelyan, Tejas Polakam, Yzabelle Go

An agent is only as good as the world it operates in, and building worlds that are realistic, accurate, and scalable all at once is the hard part of scaling RL. Every RL environment Scale builds runs on AgentEnv. Today we're open-sourcing it.

### RL environments are getting harder to build

Scaling RL takes a steady supply of tasks for models to practice on, and those tasks live inside RL environments: simulated slices of the real world with the tools, data, and rubrics/verifiers an agent needs to attempt a task and learn from it.

...

### Building Blocks and Interoperability

Most tools for agent training start from the task and build a world around it. AgentEnv’s philosophy starts from the world first, so one Environment can host many Tasks and many agents. AgentEnv is built on two core principles

Building blocks: What an Environment is made of. An Environment is built from versioned composable blocks: Environments like Slack or Gmail, an Artifact of data that populates them, and Rules (the clock, triggers, and roles) that govern how it behaves.

Interoperability: What an Environment works with. An Environment doesn't assume anything about who or what runs it. Any agent can connect to it, any sandbox can host it, and your cloud can run it, all through open protocols instead of custom glue.

#### Dynamic, Composable Environments

Environments are building blocks: In AgentEnv, an Environment is anything an agent can act on: Slack, Gmail, a help desk, a browser, a desktop program like Blender, or even a video game. Each Environment contains an Environment Card as part of the open AgentEnv Environment Protocol; a manifest of what the Environment is, which tools it offers and how to reach them.

Figure 1. (Illustrative) The Environment Card: on the left as you read it, on the right as agents read it at `/.well-known/agent-env.json`. An agent reads the card, then calls `email_search` over MCP.

Building blocks snap together: Combine a help desk, email, and customer records environments, and you get a complete Support Desk Environment. An accounting firm, an enterprise company, and a SupportDesk environment can all share the same underlying Slack and Email environments, but each will be loaded with its own data Artifact, alongside any additional environments they need. At Scale, we build entire simulated workplaces this way, with a dozen or more environments working together.

...

#### Designed for Interoperability

Agent Agnostic. An Environment's card tells an agent which tools it serves and how to reach them, over MCP, REST or a generated CLI. An agent's Agent Card, from the open A2A protocol, does the same in the other direction.

Pair any Environment Card with any Agent Card and the agent can start work, with no custom wiring. The same Task runs unchanged and consistent on Claude Code, OpenAI's agents, or any of your own custom agents.

Figure 3. The same Environment and Task run unchanged against any agent, in any sandbox. Four sandbox providers ship with the framework, and you can register your own by name.

Infra Agnostic. Build an Environment on your laptop and it runs unchanged weather in your cloud or local. AgentEnv comes with native, day-one support for AWS [S3, ECR, Secrets Manager], Google Cloud [Cloud Storage, Artifact Registry, Secret Manager] all set through a single config.toml file. In the future, we will be adding more providers for Sandboxes and Cloud support

Sandboxes are just as pluggable: AgentEnv supports four OOTB sandboxes (local Docker, Modal containers, and Modal and E2B virtual machines), and you can register your own as well.

At Scale, Modal is our default sandbox provider supporting all environments, task runs, evals and more!

### Build any AgentEnv Task, step by step

Now that we can define any world as an AgentEnv Environment, the next question is what you can do in it. The answer turns out to be almost anything. Since any slice of the real world can be represented as an RL environment, almost any goal, task, or workflow can be represented as an AgentEnv Task.

A Task is constructed as a DAG of AgentEnv steps. Each step represents a primitive action on an Agent, the Environment and more, like setting up the world, loading data, setting the clock, bringing in an agent, handing it the work, collecting what it made, grading the result with a rubric or a strict check.

Because steps snap together the same way Environments do, an AgentEnv Task isn't limited to being a traditional RL training sample.

One Task might give an agent a written brief and a sandbox with Blender, and ask it to build and render a 3D scene. There are no rubrics or verifiers; the Task is simply a way to experiment without managing the application infrastructure yourself.

Another Task might drop an agent into our support desk environment to resolve a refund for a customer named Dana, then grade its trajectory and the outcome.

Every AgentEnv step you build can be reused across any task!

...

### What comes out of the box

AgentEnv ships 48 built-in step types, covering everything from deploying an Environment to setting its Rules of the World to grading trajectories. Most RL Tasks can be built from these alone, with no new code. For the rest, you can add your own steps as plugins.

signals.title: A ~45 MB control plane for 1,000+ GPU nodes — GPUWorks is now Apache 2.0 - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
On November 5 we open-sourced GPUWorks under Apache 2.0. It's a ~45 MB inference platform that turns the GPU servers a team already has into one shared cluster, with no Kubernetes underneath.

We built it because four questions kept coming back:

- A handful of GPU servers doesn't justify a full orchestration stack.
- "Heterogeneous support" usually means a compatibility table nobody reads. Teams want to know which card runs which model today.
- GPU partitioning helps small models. It does nothing for three large models competing for one 8-card group.
- Inference accounting rarely survives contact with reality, so nobody knows which card-hours go to which app.

## What it actually does 

Install in about a minute. One command completes the platform installation and deployment; additional GPU nodes are connected from the browser console. No pre-built Kubernetes, and offline import is supported for packages, weights and runtime images. 

```
bash <(curl -fsSL https://dl.gpuworks.ai/get.sh)

```

Serve with an OpenAI-compatible API. 1,000+ launch configurations covering roughly 400 models. A configuration bundles the image, inference engine, weight version and startup parameters into one deployment.

Share one GPU pool across large models. Priority, idle-yield and scheduled-rotation policies let multiple large models take turns on the same cards. L1 sleep keeps weights in host memory, so a sleeping model wakes in about 4 seconds instead of reloading from storage.

On an 8x H20 test, cold start from NFS took 16 to 17.5 minutes; wake-up took about 4 seconds.

Grow from one node to a thousand. In a real-machine test, one GPUWorks Server managed 1,003 GPU servers, brought up 500+ inference replicas in four minutes, and pushed 69,000 tokens per second, while the server process used 9 CPU cores and 1.6 GB of memory.

Mix vendors deliberately. NVIDIA, AMD, Huawei Ascend, T-Head PPU, Hygon DCU and others, across bare metal, VMs and cloud containers. The platform filters hardware by model compatibility instead of leaving it to a spreadsheet. RDMA and Ascend HCCS links are discovered and managed automatically.

See where compute goes. Token usage and cache hit rates by API key, model and deployment, alongside GPU occupancy and card-hours per million output tokens.

signals.title: MemTensor Releases and Open-Sources MemT-1.0-Pro, a 554B Memory-Native Model
signals.excerpt:
SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MemTensor today released and open-sourced MemT-1.0-Pro, a memory-native model jointly developed with NVIDIA.

Built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra and trained using NVIDIA's Megatron-Core and Megatron Bridge distributed training infrastructure, MemT-1.0-Pro extends MemTensor's memory-native approach to 554 billion total parameters, with 59 billion active parameters. Following Nano and Flash, the release advances this exploration on a new backbone and at a larger model scale.

 

Architecture of MemT 1.0: integrating dynamic local memory and trainable hyper-memory into model computation.

MemT-1.0-Pro integrates memory into model computation, making the storage, updating and retrieval of historical information capabilities that can be learned through training.

The collaboration with NVIDIA included model adaptation, operator optimization, training-method discussions and experimental review.

Extending MemTensor's Memory-Native Approach to Nemotron

MemT-1.0-Pro uses NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-BF16 as its backbone. Its architecture combines dynamic local memory, which stores information acquired during interaction, with trainable hyper-memory components that learn how to write and read that information.

During online interaction, the backbone and trained memory-processing weights remain fixed. The model accesses historical information through dynamic memory states, without requiring the original historical text to remain in the query context. After each completed interaction, a storage procedure updates those states using a stabilized token-level mechanism based on Gated DeltaNet-2.

Continued pre-training establishes language modeling capabilities that use native memory. Post-training then uses distillation from a full-context teacher to improve memory-based responses.

Measurable Progress in Long-History Memory

In the technical report, MemT-1.0-Pro scores 41.80 on BEAM-1M, compared with 37.04 for MemT-1.0-Flash, an improvement of 4.76 points. On MemoryAgentBench, its score rises to 23.87 from 17.36, a gain of 6.51 points.

BEAM-1M evaluates ten long-history memory abilities, including information extraction, contradiction resolution, updating, preference following and temporal reasoning. MemoryAgentBench evaluates retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding and selective forgetting.

Pro also achieves an average score of 53.08 across 11 memory benchmarks, the highest among the parametric-memory methods evaluated in the report.

These results demonstrate progress within the MemT family, although Flash and Pro use different backbones and configurations, and improvements vary across benchmarks. Strong textual-memory systems remain ahead on some evaluations.

Toward Agents That Can Use Their Experience

For agents supporting extended workflows, useful memory involves more than recalling isolated facts. Following an ongoing project or service request may require retaining earlier requirements, recognizing updated decisions and applying information accumulated across multiple interactions.

These needs motivate MemTensor's exploration of native memory for persistent agent workflows. Further application testing will be needed to establish how the benchmark gains translate into end-to-end task performance.

Fixed-size memory introduces trade-offs between preserving earlier details and incorporating new information. Improving memory fidelity, selective retention and query-dependent readout remains central to further research.

Developers and researchers are welcome to explore MemT-1.0-Pro on Hugging Face.

signals.title: Harness-Specific RL Makes the Agent Loop Part of the Model · Hugging Face Blog
signals.excerpt:
Announcement: November 20, 2026 Published: November 23, 2026

...

THE SHORT VERSION

Treat a harness adapter as a versioned model-harness-task policy, and validate success and efficiency together across the exact production loop and meaningful transfer tests.

An agentic model never works alone. A harness decides how messages are formatted, which tools are exposed, when results return, how context is compacted, and when the run stops. Those choices shape the trajectories that a model sees. Training for the exact loop used at deployment therefore targets something more specific than general coding ability: it targets the interaction between model, tools, and control software.

A Hugging Face experiment applies this idea to Qwen3.8-27B. The team froze the base weights and trained separate LoRA adapters with reinforcement learning inside Pi, Hermes Agent, and OpenCode. Rollouts used the released harnesses rather than trainer-specific approximations. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and a hard SWE-bench Pro subset, each specialist beat the base model under its own harness while using fewer tool calls. The team also concatenated the three LoRA updates into a rank-96 adapter, scaling each update by one half.

The results make a strong case for treating the harness as part of the optimization target. They also suggest a more careful evaluation discipline for anyone deciding whether the approach belongs in production.

signals.title: TensorRT-LLM V1.3.0 Brings NVFP4 To Hopper And Ada, Drops Legacy Backend | Smart Chunks
signals.excerpt:
November 22, 2026

...

## TL;DR

- NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0 adds MXFP8, an 8-bit number format, for standard layers and mixture-of-experts layers.
- A new 4-bit, weight-only NVFP4 path built on Marlin means NVFP4 checkpoints now run on Hopper and Ada Lovelace GPUs.
- NVFP4 quantization is now tunable, and PyTorch is the only backend left.
- The practical upshot: more NVIDIA GPUs can serve newer compressed models.

## Two new low-precision paths and one big deletion

Quantization means storing a model’s numbers with fewer bits. Fewer bits means a smaller memory footprint. NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0 release adds two new ways to do that.

The first is MXFP8, written as W8A8. That label means the weights (the numbers the model learned) and the activations (the values it computes while running) both use 8 bits. Support covers linear layers, the basic matrix-math blocks, and MoE layers. MoE is short for mixture of experts: a model split into specialist sub-networks, where only a few work on each token.

The release notes name MiniMax-M3 as one supported MXFP8 checkpoint. A checkpoint is simply a saved set of model weights. The exact line reads: “Added MXFP8 (W8A8) linear and MoE support, including MXFP8 checkpoints such as MiniMax-M3.”

The second path is the one I’d watch. NVIDIA “added W4A16 NVFP4 weight-only quantization through Marlin, so NVFP4 checkpoints run on Hopper and Ada Lovelace.” Translation: weights are stored in 4 bits while activations stay at 16. Marlin is a set of GPU kernels, the small programs that do the actual math. Hopper and Ada Lovelace are two NVIDIA GPU generations.

The release also adds tunable NVFP4 quantization. It supports both legacy and ModelOpt 1.x quantization config formats. The notes don’t spell out what “tunable” lets you adjust.

...

And that’s the trade. You get a smaller footprint without asking every layer to run at 4 bits. The release notes don’t say how much speed or memory you actually gain, so I won’t guess.

...

## The quieter change: PyTorch is now the only backend

TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA’s open-source library for optimizing and serving large language models on its GPUs. A backend is the engine underneath that actually executes the model. Version 1.3.0 removes the legacy TensorRT backend, which leaves PyTorch as the sole backend.

That’s a major architectural change. It also means fewer code paths to maintain and test. For NVIDIA, new quantization formats now have one place to land.

For users, the picture is less tidy. Anyone whose setup still leans on the old backend will need to check their workflow before upgrading. The support for legacy and ModelOpt 1.x config formats looks like a bridge for existing quantization setups. The notes don’t say how smooth that bridge is.

signals.title: Baidu posts ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview as 280B MoE checkpoint | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
Baidu has released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on Hugging Face, a 280-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 14B parameters per token and ships under Apache 2.0. The model card describes it as "an intermediate checkpoint from post-training" rather than a finished release.

The architecture uses 43 layers (1 dense, 42 MoE) with 512 routed experts and one shared expert, and extends context to 1,048,576 tokens. Baidu says mid-training "extends the training context length from 128K to 1M tokens." Default weights ship in blockwise FP8 with routed experts in MXFP4; teams without FP4 kernels are directed to the FP8 or BF16 repositories.

On Baidu's own benchmark table, the model trails Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (46.5 to 66.4), HLE without tools (46.4 to 61.4) and AA-Omniscience-Public (25.2 to 62.0), while leading on SpreadsheetBench V2 (36.4 to 35.1) and OfficeQA Pro V2 (67.9 to 62.2). Against DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash it posts 71.2 on DeepSWE v1.1 to the DeepSeek score of 74.9.

Baidu claims the DSpark speculative decoding setup "gives a 40% speedup" at a 1M-token context, with "an average acceptance length above 5.5 on real-world multi-turn conversations" using seven draft steps. The card says W4A8 quantization-aware training keeps training and inference numerically aligned, "which removes the accuracy gap that a mismatch between them would otherwise cause."

The company positions the model for long-running agentic work. The card reports the model "wrote a complete third-person wuxia game in C++ on Unreal Engine 5.8" in a single 11-hour coding task, and that it was trained in 300,000 workspaces holding "10 million reference files in more than 40 file types." Baidu adds that "Post-training is ongoing and ERNIE 5.5 Flash is improving quickly."

The next checkpoint is the non-preview release: whether post-training closes the Terminal-Bench 4.0 and HLE gaps against Claude Opus 5.5, and whether Baidu keeps Apache 2.0 on the final weights, will decide if this is a usable open MoE or a staging post.

signals.title: DetLLM Achieves Deterministic LLM Inference with Integers
signals.excerpt:
A new technical approach called DetLLM has achieved fully deterministic inference for large language models by eliminating floating-point arithmetic in favor of integer-only operations. The research, published by Nathan Reitinger, addresses a longstanding challenge in AI systems: different hardware producing slightly different outputs for identical inputs due to floating-point rounding inconsistencies.

...

## Integer-Only Arithmetic Solution

DetLLM solves this by quantizing all model weights and activations to fixed-point integer representations. The system performs matrix multiplications, attention operations, and normalization steps using exclusively integer arithmetic with deterministic rounding rules. By eliminating floating-point operations entirely, the approach guarantees bit-identical outputs for the same input regardless of underlying hardware.

The technique builds on existing quantization methods but extends them to cover every computational step in the inference pipeline. Unlike traditional quantization that reduces precision for speed or memory savings, DetLLM prioritizes reproducibility while maintaining accuracy comparable to full-precision models.

## Release Date and Availability

Officially released on November 23, 2026, the DetLLM research and implementation are now publicly available. The project provides both technical documentation and reference implementations demonstrating integer-only inference across multiple model architectures. Early testing shows the approach works with popular transformer models without requiring retraining or architectural modifications.

## Implementation and Performance

The integer-only approach introduces minimal computational overhead compared to standard quantized inference. Key optimizations include:

- Fixed-point multiplication with controlled bit-width expansion
- Deterministic softmax approximation using integer lookup tables
- Scaled integer representations for normalization layers
- Bit-shift operations replacing floating-point division

Benchmarks show DetLLM maintains output quality within 1-2% of floating-point baselines while guaranteeing reproducibility. The technique integrates with existing inference frameworks and requires no specialized hardware beyond standard integer ALUs available in modern processors.

signals.title: Thinking Machines wows with Inkling 2 Mini looped transformer model that runs locally on laptops | VentureBeat
signals.excerpt:
Thinking Machines Lab, the San Francisco-based AI startup started and led by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, is challenging the dominant paradigm of cloud-based AI frontier models with the release yesterday of Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights multimodal model engineered to run offline on a 32GB MacBook Pro or a single desktop GPU.

At the same time, Inkling 2 Mini rivals much larger systems on software engineering and tool-use benchmarks.

At 26.4 billion total parameters and a ~20GB memory footprint, Inkling 2 Mini represents a deliberate shift in how AI labs extract reasoning performance from compact hardware. Rather than scaling parameter counts upward, Thinking Machines relies on a "looped transformer" architecture that cycles data through its middle layers multiple times per token. 

The result is a U.S.-built, Apache 2.0-licensed model that ties Alibaba's dense 27B flagship on aggregate intelligence benchmarks while running roughly four times faster and six times cheaper per task—a combination that has already drawn rapid support from local-AI runtimes and enthusiastic early reviews across the developer community.

...

Inkling 2 Mini takes a different path. According to the Inkling 2 Mini model card, the system is a 24-layer, decoder-only sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that routes each token to 8 of 128 experts, activating 3.4 billion parameters on a standard pass. The architectural twist lies in how those 24 layers execute: the first six layers (the prelude) and the final six layers run once, while the middle 12 layers run three times using shared weights. Think of it like a human engineer pausing to mentally double-check a complex equation three times before writing down the next line of code, rather than scribbling out three pages of scratch work.

Those three passes yield 48 effective layer applications per token—and 5.4 billion effective active parameters—without increasing the model's storage footprint. To keep information flowing cleanly across iterations, Thinking Machines implemented attention residuals, allowing each pass to read a gated "message" from the previous pass's middle layers alongside the initial prelude output. In internal scaling tests, the company found that a non-looping baseline required 140% more inference compute to match the looped model's loss on 512K-token agentic traces.

To make the model practical on consumer silicon, Thinking Machines pruned two-thirds of the experts mid-training (from 384 down to 128) and "healed" the network by distilling 1 trillion tokens from a larger internal Inkling model, followed by supervised fine-tuning and 2.2 trillion tokens of reinforcement learning. Crucially, the team trained and deployed the first 20 layers natively in 4-bit NVFP4 precision and the final four layers in 8-bit MXFP8 precision. Because the weights ship in the exact numeric format used during training, developers avoid the accuracy degradation that typically plagues post-training quantization.

...

Inkling 2 Mini is natively multimodal, accepting UTF-8 text and pixel-based images (optimally between 40px and 4096px) across a 1-million-token context window and outputting text. Thinking Machines demonstrated its offline capabilities by running the model in airplane mode on a 48GB M5 Pro MacBook Pro to build a playable flight simulator in minutes, as well as powering 20 persistent autonomous villagers simultaneously in a local town simulation.

On standardized evaluations, Inkling 2 Mini punches well above its weight class in agentic coding and tool use. It leads all sub-100B open-weights models on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%), SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard (77.9%), and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%), while scoring 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified and 85.3% on DeepSearchQA. On Stanford's intelligence-per-joule benchmark running on an NVIDIA DGX Spark, Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703, comfortably ahead of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (0.430) and Gemma-4-26B-A4B (0.159).

However, looping cannot conjure facts out of thin air. Because factual recall scales primarily with total parameter count, Inkling 2 Mini scores -8.6 on AA-Omniscience v1.1 (with a 63.4% non-hallucination rate), trailing denser peers like Qwen3.8-27B (-6.4 and 71.4%). Thinking Machines also notes in its documentation that the model trails Qwen3.8-27B on multi-turn chat (50.0% on MultiChallenge) and multi-constraint instructions (33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1), and can occasionally fall into repetitive debugging loops or produce clipped phrasing in non-English languages such as Chinese.

signals.title: Meko's Agentic Context Engine: Beyond Memory in Infrastructure
signals.excerpt:
## The News

ECI Research recently sat down with the leadership team at YugabyteD Enterprise to discuss the evolution of Meko, their agentic context engine, and AMP, a multi-tenant PostgreSQL offering designed for serverless, auto-scaling agent workloads. Meko has expanded well beyond its origins as a data processor for AI agents, now functioning as a unified context layer that combines vector stores, graph stores, memory, RAG pipelines, and transactional databases under a single interface. AMP addresses the database provisioning challenge that emerges when enterprises deploy agents at scale, offering a serverless approach to database infrastructure for agent workloads.

## Analyst Take

### The context problem is bigger than the memory problem

Most of the current market conversation around agentic AI infrastructure fixates on memory. Which memory layer? How does it persist? How does it retrieve? That framing is too narrow, and Meko’s positioning reflects a more accurate understanding of what agents actually need to function reliably. Memory is one input into a context pipeline that also includes artifacts, skills, structured data, and conversation history. Collapsing all of that into a single managed data pack, and then surfacing a “context quality” score to tell developers when their context is too sparse or too bloated, is a potentially differentiated technical contribution. The “context paradox” the team describes, that both too little and too much context degrades agent output, is a real architectural problem that most teams are currently solving through trial and error.

For developers building production agentic applications, this matters immediately. The alternative is stitching together a vector database, a memory layer, a RAG pipeline, and a document store independently, then hoping the seams hold under load. That is a common architectural challenge for teams today. A unified context engine with quality feedback could change the debugging surface area significantly.

signals.title: Tencent's Hy4 runs on MetaX's Chinese GPU with FlagOS W8A8 | iMasters
signals.excerpt:
MetaX says its C550 GPUs already support Tencent's flagship Hy4 model (Hunyuan), released on November 20, and published a quantized version via FlagOS. The manufacturer's own numbers show throughput gains and worse initial latency.

## What MetaX announced

Chinese GPU maker MetaX says it completed a "day-zero" adaptation of its C-series GPUs to Hy4, Tencent's flagship model, hours after the company released the model's weights for download on November 20, 2026. Alongside this, MetaX published a W8A8 quantized version of Hy4 built on FlagOS, according to a Pandaily report published on November 22.

It's important to separate two things the news bundles together. One is the hardware and software adaptation to run the original Hy4 on MetaX's C550 GPUs. The other is this W8A8 version, which is not a new model trained from scratch: it's a lighter way of serving the same weights, using eight bits for weights and activations instead of the original precision. Pandaily also notes that this release is separate from MetaX's earlier adaptation to "Hy4 flash" (a leaner variant of the same model) and from Tencent's original announcement, covered in another Pandaily report.

## MXMACA and FlagOS: the stack trying to play CUDA's role

MetaX attributes the quick integration to its MXMACA software stack, which includes drivers, interfaces, the MXCC compiler, operator adaptation, and connections to inference frameworks. In practice, it's an attempt to offer Chinese GPUs the same kind of layer that CUDA offers Nvidia GPUs: without it, running a large model on different hardware requires rewriting operator by operator.

FlagOS, behind the W8A8 version, is a BAAI (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence) project to standardize operators across different Chinese chips. Pandaily published another piece on FlagOS version 2.2, which already covers 1,454 operators across manufacturers such as MetaX and Huawei Ascend. The stated goal is to let the same quantized model run on multiple domestic accelerators without manual rewriting, which matters in a market where access to cutting-edge Nvidia GPUs remains restricted by US export controls.

## The 32-GPU benchmark: throughput rises, initial latency gets worse

The model card accompanying the release describes a cluster of four servers, each with eight 64GB C550 GPUs, totaling 32 GPUs. The test uses 64 concurrent requests, with roughly 4,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens per request, according to the report. These specific hardware and load conditions matter for interpreting the numbers, because they are not equivalent to a production test with real traffic.

| Metric | With decode-graph | Without decode-graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aggregate output throughput | 80.98 tokens/s | 52.31 tokens/s |
| Average time to first token (with queue) | 227.2 s | 220.5 s |

In other words: the "decode-graph" mode recommended by MetaX increases throughput by about 55%, but time to first token got worse, not better, when the waiting queue is counted in. Both numbers come from the same card and the same report, and together they rule out any reading that "everything improved": there is a real trade-off between aggregate throughput and latency perceived per individual request.

Two additional points limit the benchmark's scope. The deployment recipe uses a maximum context of 65,536 tokens, well below the 1 million token capacity Tencent advertises for the original Hy4, so the numbers say nothing about long-context performance. The card also marks two multimodal evaluations as "in progress," not completed.

In short: the numbers come from the manufacturer itself, specific to one configuration, and Pandaily was explicit in treating them as "vendor claims," not as independently verified results in real applications.

## What Pandaily's verification found (and didn't find)

It's worth highlighting a reporting detail that sets this coverage apart from a simple reproduced press release. The cited FlagRelease repository is public and contains weight files in safetensors format available for download, not just an announcement or a hosted demo. In the verification, a limited request managed to retrieve 64 bytes from a weight fragment listed in the repository.

Pandaily did not download the complete model or run the deployment described in the card. This means the existence of the weights was confirmed, but the performance MetaX declared was not independently reproduced.
